title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 5
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A supermarket chain replaced half of its staffed checkouts with self-service machines and reports that the average time customers spend queueing has fallen. It concludes that customers are now served more quickly.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Some customers dislike using the machines.
B. The machines occasionally require staff assistance.
C. The chain reduced the number of staff employed at each store.
D. Queueing times were measured by store managers rather than by an outside firm.
E. Many customers with large trolleys now shop at a competitor, so the remaining customers have smaller baskets.
questions.explanation: If the slowest customers left, average queueing time falls without anyone being served faster — the measure improved because the population changed. C and D would slow service, if anything, and E questions the data without offering a reason for bias.

questions.prompt: Beekeepers in the Wendale valley report that colonies placed near flowering oilseed fields produce more honey than colonies placed near mixed hedgerows. An agricultural adviser recommends that beekeepers move all colonies to oilseed fields to maximise honey production.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the recommendation?
options: A. Whether honey from oilseed fields sells at the same price as other honey
B. Whether colonies at oilseed fields remain as productive once the short flowering period ends
C. How many beekeepers operate in the valley
D. Whether oilseed is grown elsewhere in the county
E. How long bees live in each type of location
questions.explanation: Oilseed flowers briefly; a colony with nothing to forage afterwards may yield less over a season than one beside hedgerows that flower successively. A bears on revenue rather than on production, which is what the recommendation targets.

questions.prompt: An insurer found that claims submitted within two weeks of a policy's start date are three times more likely to be rejected as fraudulent than claims submitted later. The insurer proposes to investigate all early claims more intensively.
questions.question: The proposal assumes which of the following?
options: A. Fraudulent claims are more costly than genuine ones.
B. Policyholders who submit early claims are aware of the rejection rate.
C. Most fraudulent claims are submitted early.
D. The additional investigation will identify enough further fraudulent claims to justify its cost.
E. The insurer's existing investigators are underemployed.
questions.explanation: A higher base rate makes the group worth attention only if intensified scrutiny catches enough additional fraud to pay for itself. D does not follow from the premise and is not needed: early claims may be a small share of all fraud and still be worth screening.

questions.prompt: A university rose twenty places in a national ranking after increasing its spending on student facilities. Its vice-chancellor concluded that the spending caused the rise.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the vice-chancellor's conclusion?
options: A. The ranking changed its methodology that year to give greater weight to graduate employment, on which the university performs strongly.
B. Other universities also increased spending on facilities that year.
C. Students report high satisfaction with the new facilities.
D. The spending was funded by borrowing.
E. The university's research output was unchanged.
questions.explanation: A methodology change that favours an existing strength explains the movement without any effect of the spending. A weakens only mildly, since relative position depends on others' actions too.

questions.prompt: A logistics company argues that delivering parcels by drone in rural areas will reduce its delivery costs, since a drone flight consumes far less energy than a van journey to the same address.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the objection that it
options: A. ignores the possibility that customers will object to drones
B. assumes rural addresses are harder to reach than urban ones
C. treats energy consumption as though it were the whole of delivery cost
D. overlooks the weather conditions in rural areas
E. relies on a comparison with vans rather than with bicycles
questions.explanation: Vans carry many parcels per journey and their cost includes labour and capital; a per-flight energy saving does not establish a lower cost per parcel. D is a genuine operational risk but a narrower objection.

questions.prompt: Every course in the Halloway programme that requires a laboratory session is assessed by examination. No course assessed by examination is taught entirely online. Some courses in the programme are taught entirely online.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Most courses in the programme are assessed by examination.
B. Every course taught entirely online is assessed by coursework.
C. Every course requiring a laboratory session is taught in person.
D. Some courses in the programme do not require a laboratory session.
E. Courses taught online are easier than those taught in person.
questions.explanation: Online courses exist; online implies not examined, and laboratory implies examined, so those courses cannot require a laboratory - some courses therefore have none. C does not follow: not assessed by examination leaves open a portfolio, a presentation or anything else. D confuses not taught entirely online with taught in person.

questions.prompt: A publisher of academic textbooks argues that its high prices are necessary because each new edition requires substantial revision. Critics point out that the publisher issues new editions of its most profitable titles every two years, while comparable titles from other publishers are revised every four.
questions.question: The critics' point serves to
options: A. suggest that the frequency of revision may be driven by something other than the need to revise
B. establish that the publisher's costs are lower than it claims
C. show that academic knowledge changes slowly
D. argue that textbook prices should be regulated
E. demonstrate that the publisher's titles are of poor quality
questions.explanation: Selective frequency on the most profitable titles points to a commercial motive — new editions make second-hand copies unusable — rather than to scholarly necessity. A overstates: the critics undercut the justification without establishing a cost figure.

questions.prompt: A company installed software that records how long employees spend on each task. In the following quarter, recorded time on core tasks rose by 15 per cent, and the company concluded that productivity had improved.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. fails to consider the cost of the software
B. assumes that time recorded as spent on a task measures output
C. overlooks employees' objections to monitoring
D. relies on a single quarter of data
E. does not compare the company with its competitors
questions.explanation: Recorded time is an input, and one that employees now have reason to log generously. D is a fair limitation, but even several quarters of the same measure would not turn hours into output.

questions.prompt: A coastal authority built a sea wall in front of one village, and the beach in front of the neighbouring village has since eroded much faster than before. Engineers say the wall is responsible, because it reflects wave energy along the coast rather than absorbing it.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the engineers' explanation?
options: A. The sea wall was built with public funds.
B. The neighbouring village has requested a wall of its own.
C. Storms have become more frequent along the coast.
D. The wall has protected the first village successfully.
E. Erosion rates at comparable unwalled stretches of the same coast were unchanged over the same period.
questions.explanation: Stable erosion elsewhere on the same coast rules out a general cause such as changing storm conditions, which is what D would otherwise supply as a rival explanation.

questions.prompt: Sales of electric bicycles in Terring rose sharply after the city introduced a purchase subsidy. A councillor concluded that the subsidy caused most of the increase and that withdrawing it would return sales to their earlier level.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the councillor's conclusion?
options: A. The subsidy was advertised on local radio.
B. Some buyers would have purchased a bicycle without the subsidy.
C. The city also opened a network of protected cycle lanes in the same year, and surveys of buyers cite the lanes more often than the subsidy.
D. Electric bicycle prices fell nationally.
E. The subsidy is due to expire next year.
questions.explanation: A concurrent change that buyers themselves name as their reason challenges both halves of the conclusion. C weakens the causal share slightly; D offers a rival cause but without evidence tying it to these buyers.

questions.prompt: A canteen replaced its fried options with grilled ones and reports that sales of fried food have fallen to zero, which it presents as evidence that diners' preferences have shifted toward healthier eating.
questions.question: Which of the following most clearly identifies the flaw in the canteen's reasoning?
options: A. Sales figures are an unreliable measure of consumption.
B. Fried food sales fell to zero because fried food was no longer available, not necessarily because diners stopped wanting it.
C. Grilled food is not necessarily healthier than fried food.
D. The canteen did not survey its diners.
E. Some diners may eat elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The outcome is guaranteed by the change itself, so it carries no information about preferences. C and E are relevant considerations but do not name the circularity.

questions.passageText:
A chain that owns its outlets keeps all their profits; a chain that franchises them surrenders most of that income to franchisees in exchange for a fee and a royalty. The persistence of franchising therefore requires explanation, and the explanation usually offered — that franchising raises capital the chain could not raise itself — is the weakest of the available accounts. Chains typically franchise their most profitable formats, and a firm able to borrow against a proven format has cheaper sources of capital than selling a share of its future earnings.

A stronger account concerns monitoring. An outlet manager on a salary must be supervised, and supervision is expensive where the manager's decisions are hard to observe from a distance. A franchisee who keeps the residual profit supervises himself, and the value of that arrangement rises with distance from headquarters, with variability in local conditions, and with the difficulty of measuring effort. The prediction follows that outlets far from headquarters or in unusual markets are more likely to be franchised, and this pattern is broadly observed.

The arrangement has a characteristic weakness, and it is the mirror image of its strength. A franchisee who captures the profit of his own outlet does not capture the value of the brand, which is shared. Cutting quality saves him money and costs the chain reputation, and the loss falls mostly on other outlets. Franchise contracts are consequently thick with quality requirements, inspection rights and termination clauses that would be unnecessary in an owned outlet, and enforcing them consumes much of what was saved on supervision.
questions.prompt: The author regards the capital-raising explanation of franchising as
options: A. the most persuasive of those available
B. applicable only to newly founded chains
C. unsupported by any evidence
D. equivalent to the monitoring explanation
E. the weakest of the available accounts
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph, with the reason given: chains franchise proven, profitable formats, against which they could borrow more cheaply than by selling future earnings.

options: A. cannot borrow against the value of the outlet
B. receives no share of the chain's advertising

questions.passageText:
Tree rings offer something rare in the study of past climate: an annual record that can be dated exactly by counting back from the present. Where growth is limited by a single factor — temperature near the treeline, moisture in arid regions — ring width and density carry a usable climate signal, and chronologies assembled from living trees, dead wood and timber in old buildings extend the record back thousands of years in some regions.

The limitations are as important as the capability. A tree records the climate of its growing season, which in most species means it says little about winter. The signal is local, so a network of sites is required before anything can be said about a region. And the relationship between climate and growth is not necessarily stable: a tree limited by temperature may become limited by moisture as conditions change, in which case the statistical relationship calibrated over the instrumental period cannot be extended backward with confidence.

Reconstruction methods have also been contested on statistical grounds. Selecting the trees whose ring widths correlate best with recent temperature can, if done carelessly, build the expected pattern into the result, and standardisation procedures that remove the age-related growth trend can also remove genuine long-term climate variation.

None of this makes the enterprise unsound. It means that a reconstruction is an estimate carrying assumptions that must be stated, and that its strength lies less in any single chronology than in the agreement of independent proxies — corals, ice cores, lake sediments — that share none of the same weaknesses.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that tree-ring records are most informative about climate when
options: A. growth is limited principally by one factor, such as temperature or moisture
B. trees grow in conditions where several factors limit growth equally
C. the trees sampled are of uniform age
D. the record extends beyond the instrumental period
E. chronologies are drawn from a single site
questions.explanation: Stated directly. E contradicts the passage's insistence that a network of sites is needed; A describes the case in which the signal is hardest to extract.

options: A. show that tree rings are less reliable than other proxies

questions.passageText:
Workers in large cities earn more than otherwise similar workers elsewhere, and the gap has proved durable across countries and decades. Three families of explanation compete, and they have different policy implications.

The first is sorting. If more able or more ambitious workers move to cities, city wages will exceed rural wages without cities making anyone more productive. Studies following the same individuals over time find that sorting accounts for a substantial part of the raw gap, but not all of it: earnings tend to rise with time spent in a large city and the gain is partly retained after leaving, which is difficult to reconcile with pure selection.

The second is matching. Thick labour markets allow employers and workers to find better-suited pairings; a specialist finds the firm that needs precisely that specialism, and neither has to compromise. The third is learning. Proximity to many other workers and firms accelerates the acquisition of skills, which would explain both the wage growth observed with duration and its persistence after departure.

The distinction matters. If cities merely attract the productive, policies encouraging urban growth transfer income geographically without creating it. If cities make workers more productive, then constraints on urban housing supply that keep people out of large cities impose a genuine national cost — and the evidence for learning, though not decisive, is what turns a question about wages into a question about how much housing a country permits to be built.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the sorting explanation holds that
options: A. cities raise the productivity of the workers who move to them
B. workers in cities work longer hours
C. high city wages reflect the characteristics of workers who move there rather than any effect of the city
D. employers in cities pay more to compensate for higher living costs
E. urban wage data are systematically mismeasured
questions.explanation: Sorting attributes the gap to who moves, not to what cities do. D is a plausible real-world factor the passage does not raise.

questions.prompt: Which finding described in the passage is hardest to reconcile with a pure sorting explanation?
options: A. City wages exceed rural wages in many countries.
B. Large cities contain more specialised firms.
C. Housing costs are higher in large cities.
D. Sorting accounts for a substantial part of the raw gap.
E. Earnings rise with time spent in a large city and are partly retained after leaving.
questions.explanation: Pure selection predicts a level difference fixed by the worker's characteristics, not a gain that accumulates with duration and persists afterwards.

questions.prompt: The final paragraph indicates that the choice among explanations matters chiefly because it determines whether
options: A. urban wage data should be adjusted for cost of living
B. restrictions on urban housing supply impose a genuine national cost
C. matching or learning is the stronger effect
D. rural development programmes should be expanded
E. workers should be compensated for relocating
questions.explanation: If cities create productivity rather than merely attracting it, keeping people out through housing constraints is a national loss, not a transfer.

questions.passageText:
When Linear B tablets were unearthed on Crete at the beginning of the twentieth century, nothing about them was known: not the language they recorded, not the sound of any sign, not even whether the script was alphabetic or syllabic. The decipherment achieved in 1952 is instructive because so much of it was accomplished before any sound was assigned to any sign.

The preliminary work was structural. Sign counts indicated a syllabary rather than an alphabet. Alice Kober showed that certain words appeared in sets differing only in their final signs, which implied inflection and, more usefully, allowed signs to be sorted into groups sharing a consonant or a vowel without anyone knowing which consonant or vowel. This produced a grid of relationships — a map of the system's internal structure, empty of sound values.

Michael Ventris completed the grid and then made a guess: that certain frequently occurring words were place names on Crete. Fitting candidate names into the grid produced sound values which, applied elsewhere, generated words that were recognisably Greek — a result Ventris had not expected and initially resisted, since Greek was thought to have arrived later than the tablets.

The episode is often told as a story of inspiration. The more accurate account is that the inspired guess was only testable because the structural work had already constrained the possibilities so tightly that a wrong guess would have produced nothing but noise, and that the decisive evidence was the appearance of coherent language in passages the guess had never touched.
questions.prompt: The passage emphasises that much of the work leading to the decipherment was accomplished
options: A. by assigning sound values to the most frequent signs first
B. by comparing the tablets with Egyptian inscriptions
C. after the language had been identified as Greek
D. before any sound value had been assigned to any sign
E. through the discovery of a bilingual text
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes structural work — syllabary, inflection, the grid — carried out with no sound values at all. E describes the Rosetta case, which is precisely what was unavailable here.

questions.prompt: The author suggests that the decisive evidence for Ventris's solution was
options: A. the appearance of coherent language in passages the guess had never touched
B. his own confidence in the guess about place names

Selecting the trees whose ring widths correlate best with recent temperature can, if done carelessly, build the expected pattern into the result, and standardisation procedures that remove the age-related growth trend can also remove genuine long-term climate variation.

None of this makes the enterprise unsound. It means that a reconstruction is an estimate carrying assumptions that must be stated, and that its strength lies less in any single chronology than in the agreement of independent proxies — corals, ice cores, lake sediments — that share none of the same weaknesses.

readingPassages.title: Why Cities Are Productive
readingPassages.text:
Workers in large cities earn more than otherwise similar workers elsewhere, and the gap has proved durable across countries and decades. Three families of explanation compete, and they have different policy implications.

The first is sorting. If more able or more ambitious workers move to cities, city wages will exceed rural wages without cities making anyone more productive. Studies following the same individuals over time find that sorting accounts for a substantial part of the raw gap, but not all of it: earnings tend to rise with time spent in a large city and the gain is partly retained after leaving, which is difficult to reconcile with pure selection.

The second is matching. Thick labour markets allow employers and workers to find better-suited pairings; a specialist finds the firm that needs precisely that specialism, and neither has to compromise. The third is learning. Proximity to many other workers and firms accelerates the acquisition of skills, which would explain both the wage growth observed with duration and its persistence after departure.

The distinction matters. If cities merely attract the productive, policies encouraging urban growth transfer income geographically without creating it. If cities make workers more productive, then constraints on urban housing supply that keep people out of large cities impose a genuine national cost — and the evidence for learning, though not decisive, is what turns a question about wages into a question about how much housing a country permits to be built.

readingPassages.title: Deciphering Linear B
readingPassages.text:
When Linear B tablets were unearthed on Crete at the beginning of the twentieth century, nothing about them was known: not the language they recorded, not the sound of any sign, not even whether the script was alphabetic or syllabic. The decipherment achieved in 1952 is instructive because so much of it was accomplished before any sound was assigned to any sign.

The preliminary work was structural. Sign counts indicated a syllabary rather than an alphabet. Alice Kober showed that certain words appeared in sets differing only in their final signs, which implied inflection and, more usefully, allowed signs to be sorted into groups sharing a consonant or a vowel without anyone knowing which consonant or vowel. This produced a grid of relationships — a map of the system's internal structure, empty of sound values.

Michael Ventris completed the grid and then made a guess: that certain frequently occurring words were place names on Crete. Fitting candidate names into the grid produced sound values which, applied elsewhere, generated words that were recognisably Greek — a result Ventris had not expected and initially resisted, since Greek was thought to have arrived later than the tablets.

The episode is often told as a story of inspiration. The more accurate account is that the inspired guess was only testable because the structural work had already constrained the possibilities so tightly that a wrong guess would have produced nothing but noise, and that the decisive evidence was the appearance of coherent language in passages the guess had never touched.
